summary:
The week of September 7-14, 2026 confirmed that data center restriction is no longer a purely local phenomenon: governors in three Northeastern and Western states moved from rhetoric toward concrete statewide action. New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte confirmed she will seek a multi-year data center moratorium in her next budget — effective July 2027 unless she acts sooner by executive order — after ISO-New England confirmed a large data center would raise regional energy prices, while House Democrats plan a separate 24-month moratorium bill for 2027. Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont declared the state 'will not host massive AI data centers,' carving out only smaller self-supplied projects with local approval. And on September 8, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek ordered a roughly one-year pause on data center development on state-owned land — freezing easements, leases, land-use permits, and property transfers until July 1, 2027 — though she stopped short of the three-year statewide moratorium demonstrators demanded, saying the state lacks authority for one. These moves follow New York's Executive Order 62 (July) and Texas's grid-interconnection review pause (August), meaning five or more states now have some form of executive-level restriction in effect or formally planned.
The stakes on gubernatorial desks remain high. In California, SB 1168 (CPUC fair-share transmission costs), SB 886 (a separate electricity rate class for data centers), and SB 887 (environmental impact review) all await Governor Newsom's signature or veto by the end of September, and an Imperial County Superior Court delivered a final ruling this week halting a nearly 1-million-square-foot complex approved without CEQA review — a significant precedent for litigation as a check on fast-tracked county approvals. In New York, Governor Hochul has still not acted on the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) passed in June, despite mounting pressure from legislators and community groups. Arizona's statewide debate sharpened as Attorney General Kris Mayes called for a moratorium on new approvals, Governor Katie Hobbs opposed a blanket pause, and APS proposed a 45% data center rate increase — while Pinal County supervisors rejected what would have been the state's largest campus, Vermaland's 3,300-acre project near Eloy.
At the local level, the pipeline of new restrictions showed no sign of slowing. Lake County, Illinois adopted an eight-month moratorium after more than 1,200 public comments; Levy County, Florida approved a moratorium in unincorporated areas through September 2027 over Floridan Aquifer concerns; Zeeland Township, Michigan enacted a one-year pause; and Franklin County, Kansas adopted a moratorium running to the end of 2028. Christiansburg, Virginia ended by-right industrial siting by requiring conditional use permits, and Kearney, Nebraska paired approval of a 368 MW project with a ten-page regulatory package — an increasingly common 'approve but regulate' template. Proposals advanced in Gallatin (TN), Fort Wayne (IN), Jasper County and Mount Pleasant (SC), Raritan Township (NJ), Gorham (ME), Orange County (FL), Grant County (NM), and Springhill Township (PA), while Trenton, Ohio placed an outright ban on the November ballot. Charlotte staff recommended extending the city's 150-day moratorium after a survey found 78% opposition.
Trends to watch: whether Newsom signs the California rate-and-review package by month's end; whether Hochul signs New York's statutory moratorium on top of her executive order; the September 24 Grant County vote on New Mexico's second county-level moratorium; Charlotte's decision on extending its moratorium before the November 5 expiration; and the November ballot measures in Ohio municipalities. The emerging pattern is a two-track regime — executive pauses and ratepayer-protection statutes at the state level, moratoriums and conditional-use gatekeeping locally — converging on the same outcome: hyperscale projects face materially longer, more discretionary approval paths in a growing majority of states.
